utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Once again, Mr. Witness, let me warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made on the first day of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before I ask you to stand up, Mr. Whiting, let me again remind everybody, if you are not the person speaking at that time, please switch off your microphone. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During your direct examination you were asked some questions about Arkan whom you described as being, I believe, notorious and you testified about his role in the RSK in 1993. Are you aware, sir, that at the end of November 1990, he came from Belgrade and met with Milan Martic and others in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I only know about this from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you hear that in the press?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly I learned this while watching Croatian TV news covering Arkan's arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date specifically. It might have been sometime in 1991 that this information emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you recall that in fact not long after this meeting that he had in Golubic with Milan Martic he was in fact arrested and held I believe in Zagreb, and that was at the end of 1990 or the beginning of 1991? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something along these lines indicating that Arkan was there. I don't know who he met. I heard that he was in Knin and I heard that he had been arrested further up into the hills near Banija and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you heard that he was in Knin, did you hear that he was in Knin at the end of 1990, in November of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date or the time. I can't specify. It might have been in 1990 or possibly 1991. I wasn't involved myself and there was so much information circulating at the time that I can hardly be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear in connection with this information about Arkan meeting -- going to Knin and meeting with individuals that the topic of the meeting or of the discussion was about how Belgrade could assist in organising and arming the Serb rebels in Croatia? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that in the fall of 1990, there were explosives planted in Knin in kiosks owned by companies from Zagreb and Split. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it that the -- these companies were -- or the kiosks were targeted because the companies from Zagreb and Split were perceived to be Croatian companies. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've mentioned before in my testimony, explosives were planted in companies and kiosks along the Croatian coast but Serb-owned ones. That sort of reaction in Knin was merely a reaction to what was going on in the other parts of Croatia. What happened in Knin happened after similar things had already taken place elsewhere, outside the Krajina, in parts of Croatia that weren't Serb-controlled. It was only after that that such things started happening in the Krajina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I submit to you that in that answer you have attempted to justify what happened in Knin but you haven't answered the question. The question I put to you is: You would agree with me, would you not, that the explosives -- that the kiosks in Knin were targeted because the companies from Zagreb or Split were perceived to be Croatian companies. That's why they were targeted. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my intention to justify any kind of crime, in Knin or outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please listen to the question. We haven't got much time now. You've been here for far too long than you should have been. Answer the question, please, directly. You're not asked to justify. You're asked to agree or disagree with the proposition put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question is: Those kiosks were targeted in Knin because they were perceived to be owned by Croatian companies. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one possible interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there any other possible interpretation, sir? That's the reason, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I assume that it is, but only the perpetrator could tell you for sure what the motives were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, you had no problem in concluding that -- drawing conclusions about Serb companies or Serb places that were targeted on the coast. Are you having a difficulty drawing the obvious conclusions about what was happening in Knin? Given everything that you knew and what was happening, it was because they were Croatian companies that they were targeted. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified that there were obstacles or mines placed on the train tracks around Knin, and you testified about an occasion when a team from Zagreb came and went on the train and it was attacked. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware -- do you have any information about the fact that the Council for National Resistance was behind these provocations that were occurring in the Krajina, in the Knin municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it you have no information to indicate that that was not the case. You have no information either way, you just don't know about that. You don't know whether they were behind the provocations or not, that's something you don't know about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the perpetrators of those misdeeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified about some efforts at negotiations in the fall of 1990 between Serb leaders and the Croatian side, and you mentioned that the Croatian Minister of Interior was involved in those negotiations. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know that Milan Babic was the principal representative from the Serb side in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Council for National Resistance opposed those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware who the members of that council were, and I don't know what their positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another topic and that is the topic of salaries for the police in the Serb -- Serb police in the Krajina. And before I do that I want to show you a clip from an interview that Milan Martic gave in August of 1990. It's in evidence as Exhibit 4 and 5; the video is one and the transcript is the other. And we will have to switch to Sanction again for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I noticed that my screen tends to be a bit dark whenever these clips come on. I wonder if there is any way that quality could be improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember hearing Milan Martic making statements such as this in the media in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And nonetheless, you testified that from July of 1990 until the end of -- until January of 1991, the Knin police continued to receive salaries from the Croatian government. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still believe that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that it was in January of 1991, only after the Knin SUP was formed, that the salaries from the Croatian government ceased. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that in fact long before or quite a bit before January 1991, sometime before the beginning of December 1990, that the Croatian government cut off funding for the municipalities of Gracac, Donji Lapac, Benkovac, Knin, Obrovac, Dvor Na Uni, Korenica? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I believe I did not understand your question fully. Can you please repeat it for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly. Are you aware that sometime before the beginning of December 1990, the Croatian government stopped funding, stopped sending funds to the municipalities of Gracac, Donji Lapac, Benkovac, Knin, Obrovac, Dvor, Korenica? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer should now be a little more extensive. Up until November, we had been receiving our salaries from Zagreb on a regular basis through the Sibenik SUP. I'm telling you about the Knin station now. As for December we were told that the state coffers were running out of money and that we would be paid in two instalments. That was what Sibenik told us at the time. Just after, we received half our regular salaries for December. The other half was never sent. And that is the entire truth of this matter. The last half salary from Zagreb was in December 1990. I received it as did the entire Knin station. I don't know about the remaining stations such as Benkovac and Obrovac. They weren't under my jurisdiction, nor was there really much communication between us about this particular aspect. This information should be easy enough to check in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter Exhibit 36, please. It's a little small. Can you -- are you able to read it? Or maybe it could be blown up a little bit for the witness. Can you just take a moment to read this document, please? This is a document which references a meeting held on the 10th of December, 1990 and it references an earlier decision by the Croatian government to block funds for the various municipalities that I listed. Having seen this document, does this refresh your recollection that in fact before the beginning of December 1990, Croatia blocked funds for these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't jog my memory at all. I know there was talk of salaries being paid and then not being paid anymore but this was about municipal assemblies as institutions, whereas my police station got its funding from the republican level, from Zagreb, and not from the municipality, this being the reason that I'm not familiar with the detail of this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it the case that not long after the so-called log revolution began in August of 1990 that Croatia stopped paying the police in Knin and the Krajina? Isn't that when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is about. All I know are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question is about the -- is about your memory of the timing of this event. You have said that it occurred in January of 1991 and I'm putting to you that it occurred shortly after August of 1990. Would you agree with me that that's the case or that that is at least possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the Prosecutor is now applying pressure on the witness and this is going outside the bounds of cross-examination. The witness answered the question. He was shown a document and again he said it changed nothing about his position, that he knew about the police funds, and I think pressing this issue any further is a pure waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting? Your basis of the objection is that it's a waste of time? Mr. Milovancevic? Yes, Mr. Whiting, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's an extraordinary objection coming from the Defence, if I may say so, Your Honour. I think that I have not exhausted this issue and I don't think I have -- I'm pressuring the witness at all. I think I'm pressing for clarity on this topic and for what his memory is. So I think it's perfectly legitimate and a potentially fruitful line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you again, sir. You said that the cutting off of funding for the police occurred in January of 1991. I'm putting to you that it occurred shortly after August of 1990. Would you agree with me that -- either that that's the case or that that's possible and that you are possibly misremembering the timing of this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our salaries were regular up until December 1990. It is based on this that I can't agree with you. My conclusion is there had been sufficient funds up to that point and the cash flow was regular between the municipalities and the SUPs and the police stations. I don't know about the rest. I don't know about the -- all the different companies and enterprises in the area and how their funding worked. I'm telling you what I know. Everything else would be mere speculation, and I'm not here to make any speculations about that. I'm saying the truth. I'm saying nothing but the truth. And I'm merely trying to tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So are you telling the Trial Chamber that you're certain that your salaries were regular up until December of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely certain about that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the document 65 ter Exhibit 36 which is on the screen, could that be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 896.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified also that when the -- when the Croatian government stopped paying the police, that salaries started being paid by donations by citizens. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it in fact the case or maybe this is something again you don't know about, that funds from Belgrade, from Serbia, started to arrive to pay the salaries of the police once the Croatian government stopped paying the salaries? Isn't that in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is -- is this something else that could have happened without you knowing about, though? After all, in January of 1991, you were no longer in the position, I won't make reference to it, but your position had changed. Is it possible that this occurred without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- move to a new topic which is the situation of the Croat population in Knin. And still focusing on the second half of 1990, you testified that: "You could not even imagine that you would find yourself in a situation where people were freely interrupting the flow of traffic, they were carrying weapons, there were violations of law and order without any punishment." That appears at 6826. Now just to be clear, you're talking there about the Serb population in the area of Knin, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some questions about the Croat population. And you would agree with me, would you not, that in Knin municipality - and I believe you may have even testified about this yourself - that Croats made up about 10 per cent of the population in the Knin municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. I don't know exactly but I guess one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's approximately correct, whether it's 11 per cent, 9 per cent, that's approximately correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified with regard to the Croat population in Knin that from July of 1990 to January of 1991, that: "The security situation was worsening and fear was encroaching upon the people living there, both Croats and Serbs, Croats in particular because they constituted the minority. They didn't know what would become of them the next day." That's at 6822. You recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, isn't it true that the Croat population didn't just experience fear, they experienced harassment and mistreatment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could put it that way, that this was the case. But if there is an explosion near residential areas in a town, everybody is scared alike, regardless of their ethnicity. Everybody is terrorised. Everybody was in fear, afraid for their lives and their property. One could say, though, that the Croats had a slightly more difficult time than everybody else at the time in Knin at least. They felt greater fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question, though, is not about fear, sir. It's that -- my question is: Isn't it true that the Croat population experienced harassment and mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was both harassment and mistreatment of the entire population. Certainly victims were Croats rather than others, or to a greater extent than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, are you having some difficulty just saying that the Croat population in Knin experienced mistreatment and harassment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not having difficulty. It's the truth, and I'm not trying to hide from it, but one needs to understand the overall situation and I would like you to have a true picture of the overall situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, again, with respect, your job as a witness is simply to answer the questions, not to try to advocate a certain position or to try to give what you think is the correct position of the situation. Please just try to answer the questions. So as I understand it, you now agree with me, and you say it is true that the Croat population in Knin, from July of 1990 until January of 1991, experienced mistreatment and harassment. That's true, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I don't know if you're aware of page 12, line 11 to 13. He actually said that the harassment was greater than others. Or am I misreading?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I take that point. I think that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified also that the difficult position of the Croat population was not the result of actions taken by the public security station in Knin. In fact, it was the result of actions taken by the Council for National Resistance and the organisers of the barricades, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say that it was the result of the Council for National Resistance or barricades. It's a consequence of the overall situation, whereas barricades contributed to increasing their fear, because whenever they attempted to go somewhere and use the roads, they must have felt worse than Serbs passing through those barricades, worse than Serbs, for instance, when they attempted to go to Sibenik or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified that the media on both sides of the conflict, the Croatian media and the Serb media, was extremist, and just to quote what you said yourself. You said: "The media" -- there is at 6828 -- "the media, regardless of whether they were from Zagreb, from Belgrade, from Split, always featured reports where their own people would be presented as victims and it was not said that both were victims." You recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The media was at that time state-owned, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, not all, but most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Focusing on the most of them, the media that was state-owned, did the description that you gave that I just quoted apply to that media, to the state-owned media? Is that a fair description of the state-owned media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think I really understood the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question wasn't particularly well phrased. The description that you gave of the media, which I'll say is -- describing the media as being extremist, would you describe the state-owned media that way, as being -- in those terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe them the same way nowadays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not talking about nowadays. We are talking about then. Would you describe them as extremist at that time? The ones that you were describing in your evidence that was quoted to you, you are not talking about nowadays. When were you talking about? What period were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the question to relate to the period starting with 1990, 1991, and that's the period I'm talking about. I'm talking about that time, not today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you then say "nowadays"? You said here, unless you are misinterpreted: "I would describe them the same way nowadays."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then and now, with hindsight, I would say the same thing. I meant to say I didn't change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about your leaving your position and let's not refer to what that position was but -- or say explicitly what it was. But you recounted a story in your testimony by which in December of 1990 a policeman was murdered and another was wounded in the area around Obrovac, and you told us that you were ordered to arrest a Serb who had been suspected of having committed the murder. And you said that there was this incident and many other incidents and as a result you resigned from your post. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that statement and the whole thing. Maybe it was not interpreted quite precisely. It's not that we had to apprehend the suspect, the murder, but the person who we thought was connected with that, he was in fact just a passerby who was standing, who was at that time quite some way from the scene, and the police later found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me try to approach this a different way. Is it fair to say that because of the ethnic tensions in your area by December of 1990, that you found your job impossible to do and decided that you wanted to leave your position? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fair statement. And also because I felt responsible for a certain territory, while not being able to restore order, I felt it was my duty to offer my resignation and to say that I'm no longer capable of performing my duties under those circumstances. And I said all that at a meeting in MUP at the office of Minister Boljkovac and his deputy, Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in your direct examination you stated that -- you testified about being relieved, and you said -- you said that you would not be "morally responsible anymore." And that you "assumed where this could lead later." Now, just focusing for a moment on the Serb side of the conflict, is it fair to say that already by that time, in December of 1990, you could see that extremist forces were taking over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say that they were taking over. I don't know what you mean specifically by "taking over." But I can say that I was no longer capable, and I didn't feel capable any longer. Nobody came to threaten me in the police station and nobody threatened my men and I still had the support from Zagreb. That all is true. But I didn't want to go on in that way because I thought that if even more blood is shed, there would be never any reconciliation and I didn't want to be a party to that. I did not want to become somebody who would be criminally or morally liable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you said in your direct examination that you assumed where this could lead later, isn't it the case that you assumed that more blood would be shed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I assumed was my personal assumption. I thought that all these things that were going on for five months by that time were not being resolved, and I thought that the goodwill is lacking to deal with them. And that is what became the last straw, in my mind, and that's what drove me to offer my resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In January of 1991, Milan Martic became the secretary of the SUP in Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was because he was selected for that position, wasn't he, because from August of 1990 until that time, he had emerged as the leader of the Serb rebellion in the Krajina? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. I cannot make such judgements about somebody -- whether somebody is a leader of the rebellion or not. History will make that judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, you told us in -- about a speech that Milan Martic made in August of 1990 in which he said that the chequerboard will not fly in Knin or will not come in Knin "as long as I'm chief of the police." But you didn't tell us about anything else that he did from August of 1990 until January of 1991. Now, it's not your position, is it, that simply because he made that statement in the media in August of 1990 that suddenly he was selected of all the possible candidates to be the chief of the SUP in Knin, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when I said that he had stated that the chequerboard flag would not be hoisted anywhere in Knin while he was an official of the police, was reflected in that footage that we saw taken outside the police station. That film propelled Milan Martic into media attention and he became popular among the people. And as for the decision to appoint him secretary of the Knin SUP, that was a political decision made by the leadership of the SDS, of municipalities in SAO Krajina. I never attended such meetings or any such gatherings, so I do not know for what reasons they appointed him and not somebody else. Equally, 10 days before I arrived at Knin, nobody dreamed that I would be the person. Everybody thought it would be somebody else. And in the same way, I don't know how it was decided that he would become secretary of the SUP. Maybe there's a written decision we can refer to, but I cannot be the judge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I want to ask you several questions now based on what you've just told us. First of all, in your direct examination, you said that Milan Martic said in August, and I'm quoting now what you said: "As long as he was in charge of the police, the chequerboard would never get in Knin." It's at 6802. And now when you've said it again you've changed it. You said: "While he was an official of the police." Are you now changing your testimony on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am not changing my testimony in the least. I just want to make it clear that all that happened 16 years ago, and there were many events involved and I have to keep the time-line clear in my head. And when I said what I said about that film, I thought he said, among other things, the words you quoted. I meant to say that it was precisely that film that propelled him into media attention and it gave him popularity on the Serb side and odium on the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've made a reference to the fact that it's -- that it's 16 years ago. Are you having some difficulty because it's so long ago remembering the time-line, remembering the exact sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not having any particular difficulty, but without taking into account some major events, that statement in itself is less memorable than some other things. At that time, statements were much less important to me than killings, injuries and some other things. I still believe that things that people said were much less important than the killing of people. Milan Martic was at that time an official of the police of Knin, and after that he was suspended from his job, and that statement was quoted in the decision to suspend him as one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So as you -- just to be clear, as you sit here today, it is still your recollection that Milan Martic said that as long as -- and this is again what you said in your direct examination, as long as he was in charge of the police the chequerboard would never get into Knin. That's still your recollection of what he said, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that it was said as long as he was at the head of the police. He said as long as he was on the police force. So he was speaking of himself as one among equals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, in fact, now you are changing your -- you now recall it differently than a few days ago? Because a few days ago you testified that he said as long as he was in charge of the police. So is your recollection now today different from what it was a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my recollection should not be different from my recollection of a few days ago, but I -- although I may have said that his words were "in charge of," it's not true, and that would have been wrong even if he had said it. It would have identified him inaccurately. He could have made such statements from the very start, and he probably did. There must exist a recording of that statement where he said as long as he's on the police force of Knin and as long as the police of Knin itself exists. I'm pretty sure it's as long as he was on the police force, not in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if he would have made that statement simply by being a member of the police and not in charge, how could that statement affect whether or not the chequerboard flag would fly in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that would have made no difference; those two wordings had the same weight. I just can't accept it that the Prosecutor should put into my mouth such statements, although in practical terms it would have been no different if he had said, "As long as I'm in charge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After that statement was made, did the chequerboard flag fly in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not talking about 1995. I'm talking about immediately after he made that statement, for the months following the statement. I see you shake your head. I'm not quite sure what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the new flag of the Republic of Croatia did not fly at that time in Knin. It was not hoisted on top of buildings, of institutions, or masts or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Specifically not at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No where, no where, not that I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from this statement that you have now testified about and given several -- now at least two versions of, in August of 1990 can you tell the Trial Chamber any other act that Milan Martic did or any other thing that he did that led to him being selected as the chief of the SUP in Knin in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall anything that he had done to be selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that in January of 1991 Milan Martic urged the Serbs in the Krajina to return their weapons and, in fact, we looked at a document which is in evidence, it has two different numbers, 891 and 515. Do you remember this testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware that in fact Milan Martic did not support returning all of the weapons that were possessed by the Serbs? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at Exhibit 496? This is again --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you again a portion of the interview with Milan Martic from October of 1994. And if we could go to page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S, and in English the ERN is 5510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm waiting. Now we have 5510 up on the English. I was waiting for them both to be up. In the English I would draw the attention to the last answer, and it's on the screen for the B/C/S. It's the -- the answer -- and I'll just read it out: "I remember that day well. It was in January 1991 when Vasiljevic came to Knin. We talked in this very building. He tried to convince me to return back the ..." - if we could go to the next page in English - "... weapons taken from the police station that we distributed to the population." Now, sir, you'll have to tell me when, Mr. Witness, when you can't see it anymore on the B/C/S because I'm just reading the English. I think we are still -- yeah, if we could scroll down a little bit more, a little bit more, right there. "He also wanted me to give back the weapons that the people bought after selling cattle or something else from their houses. I agreed to return all the weapons we took from the police station in order to give the JNA another chance to disarm the paramilitary army." And then I want to skip down in the English to the next answer that reads "General Vasiljevic," and you'll have to scroll down a little bit on the B/C/S. Just the beginning of it appears now. Yeah. "General Vasiljevic tried very hard to persuade me that the JNA was going to do everything to protect the Serbs. I didn't trust him, though, seeing what the JNA had done so far to protect us. Fortunately I didn't allow all the weapons to be returned, neither the weapons the people bought by themselves, nor all the weapons we took from the police station. We bought some weapons from Serbs working abroad, got some from JNA Serb patriot officers secretly from the storages. We got some from people we didn't like, like Slovenia and even Croatia." Now, did you, sir, know anything about the fact that Milan Martic did not in fact all the weapons to be returned, now that you've seen that? Does that refresh your recollection about any information that you had about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, this does not jog my memory at all about what happened at the time. All I see is new information, information that I'm entirely unfamiliar with. For example, this is the first I hear of this particular event, Vasiljevic's arrival. This is probably General Vasiljevic. It was a well known name across the former Yugoslavia at the time. But I've never seen this interview before and I've never heard of this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on, then, to another topic since you don't know anything about this. And the topic is cooperation with the Croatian Ministry of the Interior. You testified that after Milan Martic became the secretary of the SUP, that cooperation with the Croatian Ministry of the Interior continued. But it's true, isn't it, that the Krajina Secretariat of the Interior declared that the Croatian MUP no longer had any authority in the SAO Krajina? Isn't that true? In January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At some point in your testimony you testified about Golubic, about a training centre in Golubic, and in your testimony it was in reference to the years 1993, I believe. You're aware, are you not, that the training camp in Golubic was set up in March or April of 1991, right? You knew that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that specifically. In terms of the time-line, I know that the training camp in Golubic was set up. I'm not sure if it was in March, April, or May. It's not something that I can remember specifically, but it was around that time that the camp in Golubic was set up. It was by May 1991, at least based on what I knew about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You knew that this camp was financed by the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. Nor did I ever say anything about that. That can't be gleaned from any of my various statements, the simple reason being I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Golubic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went to Golubic was before the war. There was a youth complex there and I was in the camp back in 1991 on the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I was just going to ask you to please focus on my question. My question was did you ever go to Golubic in 1991. So I'm sure you're anxious to get home. If you could just answer that question and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are very, very right when you say I can hardly wait to leave. You couldn't possibly be more right. I'm in a hurry to get home, and I could make things easier on myself by saying yes, yes, but I wish to offer further elucidations just in order to put us all in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, believe me I want you to give truthful and complete and accurate answers. I do. However, it's not necessary most of the time to give further elucidations. You just really need to answer the questions and then you'll get your wish to get home more quickly. So let's go back to this question: Did you ever go to Golubic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1991, when we were tasked with disarming the population in Potkonje and Vrpolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you went there simply as a kind of staging before you went to Potkonje and Vrpolje? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go to Golubic on any other occasions aside from that one in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you some more questions about Golubic after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I think we've reached the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Lest I forget, I'm not quite sure I understand what is meant by "staging," in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we were talking about Golubic and I used the word "staging." Let me see if I can clarify that. Is it your testimony that before the action on Potkonje and Vrpolje that you gathered and met in Golubic before proceeding to Vrpolje and Potkonje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so was it just -- were you in Golubic on that occasion just for a matter of hours or was it even less time than that or was it more time than that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even less time than that. There was the preparation, there was the meeting, and then after the operation, there was a dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A dinner? Was that dinner at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a dinner just after the operation. We stopped to eat at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you also testified that you don't recall being there on any -- in Golubic on any other occasion in 1991. So I take it that you did not go through training in Golubic yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarity on one point? You said yes, dinner, just after the operation. Is it therefore your testimony that you went to Golubic before you went to these two villages, and when you came back from the operation you went back to Golubic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, that special units, members of special units, were trained at Golubic and these special units were then attached to various public security stations in the SAO Krajina? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was working at the station in Knin. In the station itself, there was no room and nearby were stationed members of some special units. I remember that some police officers from Knin went to Golubic to be trained. I don't know where they were sent later, or whether police officers from other stations were being sent to Golubic for training. This wasn't something that I was involved in. I didn't even go to Golubic myself to see what was going on and I certainly took no decisions in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware that these so-called special units participated in fighting during the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to provide a specific answer to that. At that time, back in 1991, I only knew about the Knin station. Some of its members had been involved in the fighting at Plitvica, some other operations and the disarming of Potkonje. I don't know about any other operations. I don't know where they were carried out or who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you testified in respect of Bosko Drazic, and this is jumping ahead a little bit in time, that he "was busy with the special units. There is a strong military aspect to that sort of work." So later in 1992, when you went to Benkovac, did you -- did you learn then that the special units were in fact involved in military actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, when I arrived in Benkovac, I heard that some of the smaller units had taken part in military operations, but all of those were stories I heard upon my arrival in Benkovac and the stories were in relation to a previous period back in 1991 and partly in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "smaller units"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I say "smaller units," I mean groups of police officers comprising between 10 and 30 officers. Those comprising 10 were called squads and those comprising 30 were called platoons but by no means brigades or any other major units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was not about smaller units. The question was about special units. The question was: Later -- so later in -- "So later in 1992, when you went to Benkovac, did you learn then that the special units were in fact involved in military actions?" That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did learn, and I heard, but that wasn't before later on in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So please do answer the question directly. Then we wouldn't have wasted that time. Mr. Whiting, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to turn now to what happened in Potkonje. You would agree with me, would you not, that the population of Potkonje in 1991 was 95 per cent Croat and about 5 per cent Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not familiar with the exact information. One thing that is certain is that Potkonje was a predominantly Croat village. I'm not sure about the exact percentages but there were a good deal more Croats. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand you may not know the exact percentage but that percentage, when you say "predominantly Croat," would you agree that it's almost completely Croat, that is over 90 per cent Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would tend to agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you never received an order "that involved making a difference between citizens based on their ethnic, political, religious or any other affiliation." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. And I still believe that my behaviour conformed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But then just a few minutes after you said that, and actually it appears on the next page in the transcript, at 6847, you testified that you received an order to disarm the Croats in Potkonje who had armed themselves. Wasn't that an order directed at an ethnic group, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at that particular operation, I suppose you could say that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to take this one step further, you testified that in the fall of 1990, the Serb population in the Knin municipality had armed itself but that the police were unwilling to disarm the Serb population because it would pit them against the population, but the police took a different approach when it came to the village of Potkonje. There, the police was willing to act and to disarm the population. Would you agree with me that those -- the approaches in those two cases were different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the approaches were different, but the problems were different too. In the first case, you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. Isn't it -- in both cases, wasn't it a case where the population had armed itself? In the Knin municipality in 1990 it was the Serb population, and in April of 1991 we are talking about the Croat population? So isn't it the -- in fact the same problem that both populations had armed themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was true in both cases, the population armed itself. In the first case with hunting rifles, and in the second case with military rifles, and much more dangerous weapons. That applied to the Croatian population, and that was the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you -- in your mind -- well, I'm not going to press that. You would agree with me, would you not, that the attack on Potkonje had a devastating psychological effect on the Croatian population there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it true that -- that approximately 60 members of the SAO Krajina police participated in the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking. I don't remember specifically, but we might leave it at that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that during the attack on Potkonje, the police fired their weapons in the air --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I decided not to spring to my feet. Twice in a row the Prosecutor is entitled to his own position needless to say, but this is the third time in a row in relation to Potkonje that the Prosecutor speaks about an attack. At no point during the examination-in-chief did the witness define this as an attack. He defined it as a police operation to seize illegal weapons. At no point did he claim that this was an attack. So these are two very different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Given the evidence I'm not sure I appreciate the distinction, but I'm happy to use the word "police operation." That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think if -- I may be wrong here, but my recollection of the witness's testimony in chief was that he called it a disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that's correct. I'm happy to use the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true, sir, isn't it, that during the police operation on Potkonje, the police fired their weapons in the air? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's true that houses were searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's also true, isn't it, that several inhabitants were arrested and taken to the prison in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that maybe not on that day or the next day but as a result of this operation, a number of residents of Potkonje left, decided to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me, would you not, that in -- at that time period in April or May of 1991, Croats were leaving the area of Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably were, but I didn't know the people well, and I don't know anyone in particular who left. Maybe a small number left. It's probable that a small number left because Serbs were coming in from other towns who were swapping property with Croats, and those people who left were replaced by the incoming Serbs. I don't know anyone in particular who left, to be able to draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't ask you if you knew anybody in particular. And if we could look at your statement again, and I don't know if it's -- if it's available. Okay. The Trial Chamber has it. I don't know if the -- yes. Thank you. If it could be provided to the witness. And if we could look at page 4, please. It's page 4 in English and page 4 in the B/C/S. And I draw your attention to the paragraph that begins: "In April and May 1991, a search of weapons in two villages predominantly inhabited by Croats took place." Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I won't read through that paragraph but that paragraph describes the police action in Potkonje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you would look at the first sentence of the very next paragraph, please. "Croats were moving out of the Knin area."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said even earlier that it's probably true, and I suppose it is and it's probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference between saying it's true and it's probably true. In the statement it doesn't say it's probably true. It says: "Croats were moving out of the Knin area." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be 100 per cent sure, I would have had to know somebody personally and know that he or she had left. But some new people had arrived and occupied some apartments in the town of Knin, and I assume that they moved out in that way, with those people coming in to take their place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are saying to be 100 per cent sure you would have had to know somebody personally and know that he or she had left. Is it -- were you not telling the truth when you gave the statement and you said Croats were moving out of Knin area? Because you didn't know anybody personally to be Croat. So you were not telling the truth when you made the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I always thought and I always meant and I think I did speak the truth. When I gave that statement, we didn't go into details, whether I meant somebody by name or not. I was just saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, nobody has asked you for a name today. The question to you is: Is it true that Croats left the Knin area? Your answer to that question is either going to be a yes, it is true, no, it is not true. Now, if you say today that because you knew nobody personally you cannot therefore say that Croats left Knin then you must have been telling an untruth when you said in this statement that Croats left the Knin area. Isn't it logical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's logical that at that time some people were being moved out, probably Serbs. Surely, since Serbs were coming in and Serbs were not going to go to some place in Croatia, that's why I'm saying this Croats were leaving, and I stand by that statement that Croats were moving out at that time, but I said that based on those assumptions. Based on the assumption that new inhabitants were coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not being asked about your assumptions. You confirm -- do you confirm now as you sit there that Croats at that time left the Knin area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have told us today that the attack on Potkonje had a devastating psychological effect on the Croat population there. And in your statement the description of what happened in Potkonje comes right before your statement that Croats were moving out of the Knin area. Isn't it fair to say that there is a connection between those events, that the -- and I apologise, I again said the attack on Potkonje. The police operation on Potkonje and the effect that it had, that that caused people to leave? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it was the decision of the person who took down that statement that he put one paragraph before and another after. People were leaving even before the events in Potkonje and Vrpolje but it is certain that those events and the seizure of weapons in Potkonje and Vrpolje had an impact in terms of intensified resettlements of Croats away from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that during that police operation on Potkonje an individual by the name -- a villager from Potkonje named Zarko Batic [phoen] was wounded in the head with a firearm? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- I know that somebody was wounded and I think this could be the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know that he was wounded in the head with a firearm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, you were charged criminally by the Croatian government for your participation in the police operation on Potkonje; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is the first time you're hearing that you were charged criminally by the Croatian government for your participation in this attack -- police operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I personally was charged?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. You personally. Is this the first time you're hearing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing of this, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's move on to your -- the next event, and I'm just trying to -- I'm pausing for a moment to see if we need to move into private session but I don't think we do. You testified that you were relieved from your post in May of 1991. So that would have been just after the events in Potkonje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it was in late May or early June, I would include it in the major events of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were then given a lower-ranking position of being an inspector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You then describe going back to your village, and let's not name your name, and that armed patrols were instituted in your village for reasons of protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I presume that you thought then and think today that it was a normal thing to do to have a kind of village guard in your village to protect the village; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand which period you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm talking about when you went back to your village in June/July of 1991 and you testified that a village guard was instituted. I think your testimony was that it had already begun being instituted when you got there and it continued to be instituted. I take it that you thought then and think today that that was a justified thing to do under the circumstances, to protect your village with a kind of village guard, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at that time it was justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You then -- you describe a clash that occurred. And from what I could judge, from the sequence of your evidence, it seems to have occurred in August of 1991, a clash in your village with Croat forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know which clash you mean, but if you mean the first clash in that area, when a vehicle of the Croat -- Croatian police was attacked --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the clash that the JNA then intervened to establish a buffer. Do you recall that clash that you testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And am I right, was that in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that the JNA -- that JNA planes launched rockets at certain targets in Croat-held areas but that these areas were in fact empty and that the JNA planes were just trying to scare the enemy. Now, the enemy that you're referring to there is the Croat forces, the Croat police forces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That relates to Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that from the Croatian side, if rockets are being launched to scare them, that it would look like the JNA was not simply trying to intervene to create a buffer but that it was, in fact, acting on behalf of the Serb side? Would you agree that from the Croatian side that that's how things would look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree as far as that area is concerned, because I and the locals were not on the offensive in that area. On the contrary, we were on the defensive. We were withdrawing into one part of the village from which, if we were in danger, we were able to flee more easily and save our skins, whereas the forces of the ZNG, the Croatian home guard, were actively attacking. And as far as I know, there were no casualties when those planes did what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just understand the situation here? Were you part of the planes? Were you in the planes yourself or were you on the ground with the -- with the territorial authority of the -- of that area, of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time of that attack, I was on the ground with my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now you're being asked about the attack by the planes. Why do you answer about -- answer to what you on the ground were doing? The question doesn't relate to what you were doing on the ground. The question relates to what you think the Croats would have thought of what the planes did, not what you on the ground were doing. Can you answer that question, please? If you have forgotten, Mr. Whiting will repeat it for you. Have you forgotten?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He nodded. I believe it would perhaps be helpful if I repeated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you -- wouldn't you agree with me that from the Croatian side, from their perspective, if rockets are being launched into their area by the JNA, by JNA planes, that from their perspective it would look like the JNA was not simply trying to intervene to stop the fighting and create a buffer but that it was in fact acting on behalf of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic? We are waiting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He's just waiting for the interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say that the aviation fired targeting Croat territory. The Prosecutor is asking his question and building into that question things that the witness had never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did the witness say, Mr. Milovancevic, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said very clearly that they were in one part of the village where they had withdrawn, that they were under attack from the MUP and the home guard corps, whereas the JNA intervened and fired on a clearing, on empty ground, in order to stop this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe we should go to the text and quote that, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I'll quote the text. It's transcript 6866, and this is during direct examination on the 21st of August. And the witness said: "And one thing I can say is that in the afternoon, JNA fighter planes in two pairs, two by two, flew over the area and rocketed certain targets in the Croat-held area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you're listening, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "We realised that the planes were firing missiles into empty areas. There were no soldiers there or anything. I thought all they were trying to do it was to scare the enemy to keep the conflict from spreading." And I believe in my question I accurately quoted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. I'm being informed that what you just read out now was in private session, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That may be so, but I don't think that there is anything in there that would identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think so either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'll -- out of fairness to you, because we've had an interruption, I'll put the question to you again so you have in it mind. Wouldn't you agree with me that from the Croatian side, from their perspective, if rockets are being launched into their area by the JNA by JNA planes, that from their perspective it would look like the JNA was not simply trying to intervene to stop the fighting and create a buffer but that it was in fact acting on behalf of the Serb side? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a question for a Croatian witness, somebody who was involved in that operation. How could the witness who was just defending himself know what Croats felt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not inclined to repeat the question again, unless you want me to, Mr. Witness. Are you able to respond to the question? Would you agree with me in what I said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in your view, acting to create a buffer and to stop the conflict includes attacking one side or the area of one side in order to scare that side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the Yugoslav People's Army was at that time attacking the party that was attacking; whereas my side, the side I was on, did not need to be militarily engaged by the JNA because we wanted the attack to stop. We wanted peace. When two men are fighting, you don't need to hit the one who is lying on the ground without offering any resistance. That's how I see the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll move on. You returned to the Knin police station in October or November of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about Bruska and what you learned about Bruska, what had happened in Bruska. You testified that when you went to Benkovac in April of 1992, you went through files to familiarise yourself with the overall situation in the Benkovac municipality. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you were asked by the Trial Chamber, by His Honour Judge Hoepfel, about the investigation of the massacre in Bruska which had occurred in December of 1991, and you responded: "There was information to indicate that the massacre at Bruska had been committed by mistake by a Croatian sabotage force that had been infiltrated into the area." Now, sir, you know perfectly well, don't you, that the surviving victims of the massacre identified the perpetrators as being members of the SAO Krajina Police? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question is capricious. None of the damaged partners who were survivors of the incident gave the names of the perpetrators, and to infer that the victims identified the perpetrators is entirely inaccurate. They only spoke about what sort of clothes the perpetrators were wearing and how they had introduced themselves; that is, as belonging to the police or not belonging to the police. But not a single perpetrator was ever identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say anything about a perpetrator being identified. I said exactly that, that they were identified as being members of the SAO Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, in other languages, this word "identified" maybe means specific identification. I would also understand that in German, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. I didn't appreciate that. I certainly did not mean to say that the specific perpetrators had been identified, only that they had been described as members of the SAO Krajina Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend failed in fact to say that they were identified as Krajina police officers. He just told the witness that the perpetrators had been identified by the victims. This is a very specific claim and that was the claim that I was responding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let us look at the transcript, Mr. Milovancevic, because I don't think ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour there may have been an interpretation issue, and I can try to rephrase. To expedite the matter, I can just rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rephrase, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's begin again. You are -- you're aware, aren't you, sir, that the surviving victims of the massacre described the perpetrators as being members of the SAO Krajina Police; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is really the first time you're hearing of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truly, this is the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look, please, at Exhibit 134 in evidence. This document is a little difficult to read, if we could just blow it up a little bit. Now, this is a -- this is an official record from the Benkovac Public Security Service from the 25th of December, 1991. And it's a -- records a -- information given by one of the survivors of the massacre, and if we could just scroll down -- my question is going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on this document and the witness's answer, it is quite obvious that the witness was not physically present at the Benkovac public security station at the time this event occurred and that was what the witness said. He said: "I know nothing more about this event." He said he knew about certain aspects about what happened but by no means the event in its entirety. I'm not sure what the foundation is for the Prosecutor to be showing the witness this particular document, especially given the fact that the Defence did not delve into these particular aspects during our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say these frequent objections disrupting the cross-examination, I would really object to. This objection is baseless. The foundation for the question is that the witness testified that he reviewed the files in Benkovac when he came, and he in his direct examination gave us information, his knowledge, what he had learned about who the alleged perpetrators were. And so that is -- I'm going to ask him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The alleged perpetrators that are dealt with in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The alleged perpetrators of -- that are mentioned also in this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
