utterances.text: Well, no. He identified different alleged perpetrators. And so my question is going to be: Did he see this document, was he made aware of it, did he have information about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again, I just don't see the foundation. I don't see the foundation to pursue this matter since the witness wasn't working there, since he wasn't in charge of the investigation, since he knows nothing about it. Today, in cross-examination again we find him saying, "I know nothing about that" in addition to having such and such information, which is, after all, information that he has already shared with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may not see the foundation. The Chamber does see the foundation. The witness said he read the files, and the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you had an opportunity to read over this document, and do you see in particular that the victim describes somebody knocking at the door and an unfamiliar male voice responded: "The police, the police," and then again responded, that same voice responded: "The Krajina Police"? Do you see that in the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your review of the files in Benkovac in April of 1992 and thereafter to familiarise yourself with cases that were going on, did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember ever saying in my statement that I had gone through the files. I was in fact just familiarising myself with all the different cases, and these are, after all, two very different things. I would not have been physically able to go through such an enormous amount of different cases. I was no miracle worker. I couldn't just have looked at a file and known immediately who the perpetrator had been. I couldn't have issued orders to that effect as a result. My associates were with me at the time. They were in charge of certain investigations, and they were the persons familiarising me, giving me a low-down on what exactly what is going on. When I said I was familiar with that, that was precisely what I had in mind. By no means was I implying that I had gone through every single file. Those were literally mountains of files and there was no way I would have been able to go through all of it. What I shared with you I shared in the best possible faith and to the best of my knowledge and ability. And that applies in relation to this and a whole series of other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you, if I may. I'm going to read to you what you said on direct examination, which is why I asked this question, and you confirmed it in fact just a few minutes ago in your cross-examination. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, there was a little bit of a concern from Judge Hoepfel that shouldn't we go into private session? I didn't see the need but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would like to go more into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that these questions in the direct examination were in private session, his knowledge. I think as long as -- basically we stayed away from his position. But if the Trial Chamber or the Defence believes that we should move into private session, I'm happy to ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe let's do just so that at least we will still know what is taking -- May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the UN civilian police or UNCIVPOL. You were asked if UNCIVPOL had powers to conduct their own investigations on the ground, and your response was: "I don't know what powers they had. They never told us." But didn't you know that the role of UNCIVPOL was a strictly monitoring role? They did not -- their job was not to investigate crimes? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the civilian police of the United Nations, I know what they told me, and I know about the work we did together. What they did independently of me and my men, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. But my question is they had a strict -- their function was only to monitor what was happening and what the police were doing. They did not have a function of investigating crimes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about events that occurred around Benkovac after April of 1992, because that's where you were, and presumably that's the area that you have information about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at Exhibit 729? And this won't be broadcast, so there is no -- we just won't -- there is no danger about compromising your identity, and we can remain in open session. I'm just going to ask you, please, if you would, to look -- you see there is one, two, three, and three says, operations -- "operational." And then there is a big Roman numeral one underneath that. Sir, if you could just -- yeah, that will make it easier for you to read it. Yeah, keep going down, down, down. All the way down. There. If you could just read that -- what's written under "operational" and tell me when you get to the end of the page, and I'm going to ask you when you're done with it if it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could also blow up the English version for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The monitors of the civilian police from Kistanje accompanied by the local police visited" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. I'm sorry, I should have been more clear. You can just read it to yourself; you don't need to read it aloud. Just read that section to yourself. And could we blow up the English to have the bottom of the page -- to make it more legible? I guess we have control over the English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Could we turn to the next page on the B/C/S? And if you could just finish reading that last sentence there. Is what is written there accurate? And just so the record is clear, again we are looking at Roman numeral I of part 3 of the report. Sir, did you finish reading that, just that first section, section I of this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's difficult to say whether it's accurate or not. A lot of time has elapsed. When I look at this report, I can't see which period of time it's in relation to, especially in reference to between 11 and 17 dead, as stated by myself, allegedly. But I can't remember informing the civilian police about any rapes in the area. Believe me, throughout my time in Benkovac I never heard anything about any rape. I can't for the life of me remember anything about any rapes except --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to -- except what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for one particular case of rape that was falsely reported by a Serb lady, an interpreter who was working with the UNPROFOR CIVPOL. She reported a member of the Kenya Battalion as having raped her but that was a false report. I can't remember any rapes being committed regardless of who the victims might have been, in terms of ethnicity, Croat or Serb. I simply can't remember. Nor do I remember myself reporting anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the first page of the B/C/S translation, and perhaps I should have told you that this report has a date of the 22nd of February, 1993. Now, now that you know the date of the report, does that help you recollect anything in this report, or are you still unable to remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm looking at the date, and I know that this was a month after the attack on the villages in Benkovac municipality, after Maslenica 93 operation. I know that there were murders of Croat civilians. At the time, as I described earlier, there were many refugees roaming about town in search of accommodation. The Benkovac Crisis Staff helped with having some Croats from the area resettled else where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt you because you've provided this information in your direct examination. And my question really is now that you know the date, can you tell us whether what's written there in that first section that you read is accurate? About the report of 11 and 17 Croats have been murdered and one woman raped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number of those killed. There were Croats who were killed at the time. I've already explained about this alleged case of rape. I'm not sure which period of time this report is in reference to. The date is there but I'm not sure which period it covers and how long the period is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the last sentence. Well, could we scroll down, please, on the B/C/S? The -- do you see the sentence there where it says that a certain person confirmed information that for the past week, referring presumably to the week before the 22nd of February, 1993, between 11 and 14 -- 11 and 17 Croats have been murdered and one woman raped? So now that you see that it's the week prior to the report, does that refresh your recollection that this, in fact, occurred and was reported as described in the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clarifies the situation to some extent. But it leads me to believe that whoever wrote this did not draw a clear distinction between the area covered by my station and the area that other stations were in charge of, especially Obrovac and Kistanje. Try as hard as I might I simply can't remember that over such a brief period of time, even in February 1993, within a single week, between 11 and 17 Croats were killed. This figure itself, 11 to 17, it's quite a range, isn't it? 11 is a lot. But if I had told the civilian police anything about this, I would have tried first of all to ascertain a more accurate figure. 11 to 17 is quite vague, and if one deals with a crime, one necessarily tries to be more specific than that as a police officer, and I certainly would have. It seems quite a random figure. There were killings when all of these things were happening, but I can't remember a single case of rape for as long as I was in the area. There were killings, there were murders at the time, but I can't say exactly how many such incidents occurred because I simply don't have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that with respect to that sentence of the 11 to 17 being reported, you've given some information about the range and so forth, but is it fair to say that you don't recollect that being reported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we turn to the next page? And I'm going to ask if you can read to yourself the next section, section II of the report. If you could just read that paragraph, section II, and then I'll ask you the same question, if you can tell us whether that's accurate or not and whether you recall it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it accurately described in this paragraph, section II of the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I would lend credence to this information. There is no reason why it shouldn't be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to a previous answer, you said that the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was the only existing -- one of the only existing legal armed units in the Krajina. But you're aware, are you not, that the -- under the Vance Plan, the Krajina was supposed to be demilitarised, meaning no armed forces. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that under the Vance Plan no army was allowed in the area. I do believe, however, that the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established sometime after the aggression on Ravni Kotari and Maslenica. I'm not sure about the dates but, yes, it must have been later on. Because up until the attack the only thing that there had been was the Ministry of the Interior. There were two different kinds of formation: Units that were in charge of policing, police work, and special purpose units, whose task was to watch the borders, to a lower extent, and also to cooperate with the civilian element of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: With the military element of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, now I have to say I'm a little confused, because the attack on Maslenica was in January of 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the -- in fact, the army was declared by -- established by Milan Martic, I believe, in May of 1993; isn't that correct? As you say, after the attack on Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after the attack on Maslenica that the army was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, May 1993 is after the attack on Maslenica. Well, I'll come back to this question, these questions, later. Now, you testified that in 1993, Serb refugees -- this is: "Serb refugees would come to their homes," and their homes in context refers to Croat homes, "and take their homes by force, move in by force." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified also that in Benkovac and Knin there were very few officers to deal with these problems. You remember that testimony? It was at 6915.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is a problem with the interpretation. You probably meant -- what you probably meant to say is that there were very few soldiers, members of the army, to deal with these problems, not officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm just reading from the transcript, and it's at 6915 on the 22nd of August. "I later heard that this was the case in Knin, and other villages around Knin such as Vrpolje were experiencing some degree of difficulty because Serb refugees would come to their homes and take their homes by force, move in by force, in order to have somewhere to stay, a roof over their heads. In both Benkovac and Knin, there were very few police officers remaining in the area to uphold law and order and to deal with the sort of problems that the police usually have to deal with, that is, that constitute usual police work." So is it not your testimony that there were very few police officers to deal with these episodes of Serb refugees taking homes belonging to Croats by force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I now understand your question. The first time around, the interpretation quoted the word "officers" not policemen. When one speaks about this period, that is after the 22nd of January, 1993, most regular policemen, both in Knin and in Benkovac as well as in Obrovac and throughout the area, including Vrlika, because by this time the front line at Peruca had become active near Sinj. They were all busy with the ongoing combat operations, and we had all received orders to join the fray in numbers as great as possible, because we were few, and at the time the priority was to check the advance of the Croatian army. In practice, this left very few policemen in the towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short. The Chamber has a few housekeeping issues to talk about before we knock off. Just stick to the question please, very short and very concise and very succinct. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I just will ask one follow-on from that last answer, and that is: When you received these orders to join the fray, that is the fighting, who did you receive the orders from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll obviously need a redaction of that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you understand that secretary -- the Secretary Prijic received his orders from Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now just to go back to what we were talking about, you said just a moment ago that in practice this left very few policemen. So just to be clear about your testimony, it's your testimony that there were very few policemen who were available to deal with this problem of Serb refugees taking the homes of Croats by force. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my testimony, that there were few policemen, too few to prevent --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one more question and then if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. I was just stopping him from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But yet you've also testified that there were officers, there were -- there were policemen available to escort Croats out of the RSK as far as the Zemunik airport. And that's at 6916. Isn't it really the case that there were officers available to help Croats leave but not to help them stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really have to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just answer the question. We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just answer the question: There were officers, there were policemen who were -- there were policemen available to escort the Croats out of the RSK but there were not policemen available to help them stay in their homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on everything that the witness has said to the Prosecutor in the past few minutes, he cannot be expected to say yes or no to the question phrased this way. It is a complete misrepresentation of everything that this witness has said so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer the question. I said just answer the question. I didn't say say yes or no. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't think I did, and I also don't think that there has been any misrepresentation of what the witness has testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. Proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just answer the question, please. There were officers -- there were policemen available at that time to escort Croat civilians out of the RSK but there were not policemen available to help them stay in their homes. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you can answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful that the Court wants a little time. I can tell the witness I'm very close to finishing my cross-examination. But I can't finish it today. I'll need to finish it tomorrow. But I think this would be a convenient time, if the Court wants some time to do housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Milovancevic? There were filings to be made by yesterday. I just want to find out what the status is of those filings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just because the witness has been here a long time, can we excuse him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness please be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. You asked me whether the deadline passed yesterday. That's correct. And we complied with the order of the Court. We supplied the list of documents referred to by the Defence in our opening statement. We supplied notification of witnesses whom we would not be calling. And that's how we complied with the order. I was waiting for this issue to be raised in order to provide some additional information concerning Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milovancevic, there were a number of things to be done. You have told me about two things. You were going to -- yeah, one of them is Mr. Martic, his 65 ter summary. You have now told us about -- let's take them one by one. What is the position about Mr. Martic's testimony 65 ter summary? Is it filed or not filed? And once again, you can answer me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have a reason. Following the course of the examination of witnesses who testify about a relatively limited period of time, like the witness who was just left the courtroom, the Defence team has realised that the questioning, the examination of Mr. Martic, would be extremely lengthy and that is the reason why we took the position, after consulting Mr. Martic, that he should not appear as a witness in his own case. The issues that Mr. Martic was to testify about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the answer. The reason you don't -- you didn't have the 65 ter is that he's not going to testify. Just say that, Mr. Milovancevic. We've got a very short time. Now you're placing it on record officially that Mr. Martic is not going to testify, so we are now back to 53 witnesses and not 54. Okay. Now, what is the position about -- you said the seven who have no 65 ter summaries. You may have mentioned them a little earlier, but can you just recap me very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have the submission that we have sent in front of me, but out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that list, the Defence will not be calling four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have seen -- I have seen that filing where you say four witnesses are not being called. I just want to find out about the three. Okay. Your 92 bis lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of the witnesses mentioned, seven or six, we would not be calling four. Two witnesses from abroad should go in through 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, we have dealt with the 7. I'm talking about your 92 bis list of your entire witnesses. We are done with the seven witnesses. What is the story -- have you filed your 92 bis lists for your entire witness list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence believes that there are no witnesses who do not testify about the activities of the accused. If they do testify to the activities of the accused, they cannot go in through 92 bis. They have to go in live. Some of them will take more time, some will take less time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, it is my view that the witness before this witness, Mr. Licina, said virtually nothing about Mr. Martic, virtually. Certainly not during evidence-in-chief. Maybe Mr. Martic was mentioned once in cross-examination. That's an example of a witness who could have come in through 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence begs to differ. We are required to prove that something that the Prosecutor doesn't wish to prove does not exist. In keeping with the practice of the Tribunal, it is not up to the Defence to prove that there was no joint criminal enterprise, and that's precisely what Mr. Martic is charged with. All the things that Mr. Licina testified about relate to the existence or non-existence of the joint criminal enterprise. That is the core of the issue in the view of the Defence, not the rest. The rest will be established very easily. The question is what about the plan of the joint criminal enterprise? The witness can tell us about which victim was killed in which village in order to come to the conclusion that there was a joint criminal enterprise. We are trying to prove a completely different theory through our witnesses, and we believe that witnesses should appear live, especially on the issue of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecutor did not offer a single piece of evidence about the joint criminal enterprise in the five and a half months of his case. And that is precisely the reason why Mr. Martic is in detention now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously, if the Prosecutor has not offered a single piece of evidence, what are you disproving? All you have to say -- okay. Anyway, that's how you conduct your trial. Is it your position, therefore, that you're not filing any 92 bis lists? Mr. Martic -- I beg your pardon. I'm sorry, Mr. Martic. I want to say Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, we believe that two witnesses can testify to that issue in that way, and those are witnesses from France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Translations of exhibits in the list. You were supposed to say which ones are dropped and which ones are not dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think all that has been done. According to the information available to me now, things stand precisely as I presented them to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the expert reports that were supposed to have been provided on the 14th of August, what about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the issue we discussed at the session when you gave us the deadline of the 23rd. And we informed you then, and I understood the Trial Chamber accepted it, and the Prosecution agreed, that the military expert's report, which is being translated and should be ready in early September, will then be submitted immediately to the Prosecutor. As for the other expert, the political expert, we still have not received a decision from the Registry to appoint that person. Everything has been prepared pending that decision by the Registry. It's a technical issue. It is not overly concerning me only because the report is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it overly concerns the Prosecution and the Chamber. Bear that in mind. If I can go back to the 92 bis list, when can the two that are going to testify in terms of 92 bis be expected to be filed? Or have they been filed? The people from France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment, it is our agreement in -- within the Defence team to have that done by yesterday. And I think that it was done. I'm sorry, I don't have this material in front of me now. I don't want to be mistaken, but the information I have is that it has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the answer. That's the whole paragraph is no answer. I don't want to know what is the agreement within the Defence force. I just want to know whether it's done or not done. That's all. I know we are delaying Judge Nosworthy and we have got to move very fast. Protective measures is the last issue. I think there had been an indication that you are going to make, I don't know, a composite motion. Are you going to be dealing with them one by one as you go along? I'm not sure what the issue is about the protective measures. Can somebody remind me? I've got it on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My memory is that issue has been addressed. I don't have a memory of that being an outstanding issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One last thing. I raise it, I'm not discussing it because of time constraints, I'll probably talk about it tomorrow before we start, is the time that's been taken on witnesses as against the estimated time. And that also as against the time stipulated in terms of 73 bis. We will talk about that tomorrow. Court adjourned. Reconvene tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
